32.text: Timing matters in this lab because the KV cache is the optimization that makes autoregressive decoding practical.

35.text: PyTorch gives us the same baseline model as before. The important difference is that attention can now remember yesterday's K and V instead of recomputing them.

36.text: Nothing dramatic changes in the layer stack. That is the point: the speedup comes from preserving history, not from inventing a new model.

37.text: Softmax and loss stay ordinary. What changes is how much of the prefix attention has to rebuild at each decoding step.

105.text: This is the crucial reuse step: old keys stay alive, and only the new key is appended. The history grows without being recomputed.

106.text: Values follow the same pattern as keys, completing the cached prefix. The new token now sees the full past through reused K/V rather than rebuilt K/V.

108.text: Save the updated cache for the next step, it grows by one position each time.

109.text: T_total = total sequence length including cached positions.

111.text: Attention: Q is (B, heads, T_new, hd), K is (B, heads, T_total, hd). The result is (B, heads, T_new, T_total).

113.text: Build the causal mask with torch.triu: each new query at absolute position T_total-T_new+i can attend to all positions up to and including itself, but not beyond.

114.text: Replace scores for future positions with negative infinity. After softmax, these become exactly zero, enforcing the causal constraint that tokens cannot peek ahead.

117.text: Weighted sum of values and reshape.

121.text: The two-layer feed-forward network, unchanged from previous labs. The MLP operates per-position and does not need any caching since it has no cross-position state.

124.text: Project each token's representation into a 4x wider hidden space for richer computation.

127.text: Run the input through the two-layer feed-forward network with ReLU activation.

131.text: Transformer block, now threads the KV cache through.

134.text: Normalize activations before the attention sublayer. Pre-norm keeps gradients well-behaved and is the standard in modern transformers like LLaMA.

135.text: The attention sublayer, now accepting an optional KV cache. When a cache is provided, it only processes new positions and prepends cached keys and values.

177.text: Use CPU for this tiny model since it trains in seconds without a GPU.

254.text: Subsequent steps feed only the last token. This is the key optimization, one token instead of the full sequence.

256.text: Attention ops: T_new * T_total per head. With T_new=1, this is just T_total, linear, not quadratic.

257.text: This is the entire payoff of the lab in one line: feed one fresh token in, get one larger cache out. The old prefix survives as state instead of being rebuilt from scratch.

270.text: Disable gradient tracking for both generation methods so the comparison is fair and neither wastes time computing gradients during inference.

271.text: Start the wall clock for the naive path. Read the number it produces with suspicion: at one layer and 16 dimensions the arithmetic the cache removes is smaller than Python's per-call overhead, so this timer is mostly measuring the interpreter.

272.text: Generate 20 names with no cache, recomputing the whole prefix at every step, and return the exact attention-operation count alongside the names. The count is the measurement that matters here; the stopwatch is along for the ride.

275.text: Time the cached path the same way, over the same 20 names and the same seeds. Both loops make the same number of forward calls, so the fixed overhead cancels and only the shrunken attention term is left to show up, and at this scale it does not.

281.text: Verify the outputs are identical, since the cache is an optimization rather than an approximation. Same model, same weights and same random seed give the same output.

282.text: Side-by-side comparison of every generated name.

283.text: Flag any mismatch (there shouldn't be any).

292.text: The headline is a count of work actually performed, so it is exact and reproducible on any machine. Wall clock comes later, with caveats.

295.text: 4.3x fewer attention operations over these 20 names. An operation reduction is not a speedup: the projections, the MLP, and the Python around them are unchanged, so this bounds the win rather than reporting it.

300.text: Evaluate the closed form at T = block_size so it can be reconciled with the measured count. The two disagree, and the reason is worth a line rather than a hand-wave.

301.text: Average decode steps per name, measured rather than assumed. These names stop on BOS after about 5.8 steps, so generation never reaches position 16 and the formula's T = 16 was never the right input.

304.text: Naive: sum of t^2 for t=1..T = T(T+1)(2T+1)/6. Cubic growth.

305.text: Cached: sum of t for t=1..T = T(T+1)/2. Quadratic growth.

306.text: The ratio grows linearly with sequence length, longer sequences benefit more from caching.

307.text: Print measured against theoretical and then explain the gap, instead of quietly reporting whichever is more flattering. 4.3x versus 11.0x is not an error in either number.

310.text: Re-evaluate the same (2T+1)/3 at the observed 5.8 steps and it lands on 4.2x, right where the counter did. The saving grows with sequence length, so a corpus of six-letter names sees the very small end of it.

317.text: End-to-end wall clock, reported because the reader will want it and then immediately qualified. This ratio has been seen anywhere from below 1.00x to a few x on the same code, because it moves with machine load, which is a fact about the benchmark rather than about the cache.

320.text: Labelled 'not a speedup figure' in the output itself. Twenty six-letter names on a 16-dimensional model is a measurement of dispatch overhead with a little attention arithmetic hidden inside it.

321.text: Rather than explaining away an unhelpful number, the lab says what the number is measuring and then fixes the benchmark below. That is the more useful lesson: the optimization was fine, the experiment was wrong.

360.text: A time budget rather than a repetition count. No single count serves this table: a cached call is microseconds, where five reps measure mostly noise, while a naive call at T = 2048 can take a large fraction of a second by itself.

365.text: Take the fastest of many runs, not the mean. Anything else sharing the CPU can only ever make a call slower, so the mean measures the machine's mood while the minimum measures the code.

367.text: Seed the running minimum at infinity so the first iteration always wins, and count the reps so the table can show how much evidence is behind each cell.

369.text: Repeat until the budget is spent, subject to a floor and a ceiling. A cell that lands on the floor did so because one call already costs more than the whole budget: fine when that call is tens of milliseconds, a reason to distrust the number when it is microseconds.

372.text: One timer around one call, then keep the smallest. Loop overhead sits outside the measured region, so it cannot contaminate the number the way an outer average would.

377.text: The second defence: median across independent runs, so one throttled run cannot set the reported number. Minimum within a run, median across runs.

379.text: One untimed call per path first. The first allocation of a large tensor and the first pass through cold caches are one-time costs, and whichever path is measured first would otherwise absorb them.

384.text: The section that finally demonstrates the effect: measure the one thing that actually shrinks — the attention module for a single decode step — on synthetic tensors, so nothing about training or weights is in the way.

388.text: A fresh attention module on random activations is enough, because timing depends on tensor shapes rather than on trained weights. Reusing the trained model would have tied this benchmark to block_size = 16, which is precisely the length where the effect is invisible.

391.text: T = 64, 256, 1024, 2048. Sweeping the context length is what turns a single ambiguous ratio into a curve, and a curve you can see the shape of is worth more than any one timing.

392.text: The naive input: the whole prefix, re-projected and re-attended from scratch, giving a T x T score matrix.

393.text: The cached input is exactly one position. This is the asymmetry the whole lab is about, one row of queries against the full history instead of T of them.

394.text: A synthetic cache of the right shape stands in for a real one. What is being timed is the 1 x T attention and the cache concatenation, and neither cares whether the stored keys are meaningful.

398.text: Best-of-N for the naive step: recompute Q, K, V for the whole prefix and run a T x T attention.

399.text: Best-of-N for the cached step: one position's Q, K, V against the cached prefix, a 1 x T attention.

402.text: Print the measured ratio next to the theoretical T. On this box it climbs from under 2x at T = 64 to several hundred times at T = 2048, the right shape and comfortably short of theory.

406.text: The curve grows with T because naive attention is T x T against the cache's 1 x T. It stays under the theoretical T because the projections and the fixed per-call overhead do not shrink at all.

414.text: Both columns time work that grows with T, so both must grow with T. The lab checks that instead of asserting it — an earlier version of this benchmark reported a cached time that fell from 342.9 us at T = 1024 to 259.1 us at T = 2048, which is impossible, and nothing in the output flagged it.

447.text: At 2048 context (2T+1)/3 is 1366x fewer attention operations, and the next sentence exists to stop that being read as a 1366x speedup. Projections, MLP, and the memory traffic reading the cache back do not shrink by that factor.

451.text: The end-to-end win is large enough that no serving system ships without the cache, and it stays smaller than the operation count, bounded by whatever does not get cheaper. Past a few thousand tokens decode is memory-bound rather than compute-bound, so the bound is real rather than pedantic.
